harvest_note: Mechanisms harvested from fetched primary docs/papers/blogs only. Sources marked unreachable are listed in the .md. Every pattern carries a concrete hermes-day build spec grounded in the real module surface: hday_gate.py (pre_tool_call judge, mandate, intent_consistent, risk), hday_ctxscore.py (vacuum: keep needles / collapse junk / archive hidden chunks / head-tail degrade), hday_router.py (lexical_judge, rank_wide, rerank, Pick, suggest), hday_manifest.py (build_manifest, persist, load, stale_after), hday_gotchas.py (sections_for), __init__.py hooks (pre_llm, pre_tool_call, pre_verify, post_tool_call), the approval/decision ledger, and patches/ desktop cockpit.

patterns.name: path-addressed-memory-blocks
patterns.what: Memory is a git-backed repository owned by the agent and projected onto the runtime filesystem (MemFS / 'context repository'). Each memory is a Markdown file with YAML frontmatter and is addressed by path: the memory labelled 'system/persona' projects to system/persona.md. Files under system/ are loaded into the system prompt on every turn; everything else stays out of context until read. The file TREE is always in the system prompt, so directory and file names act as signposts the agent follows. Edits are local until committed and pushed, at which point they become the agent's memory everywhere.
patterns.why: Splits memory into a tiny always-resident core (identity, durable preferences, critical workflow rules) plus an unlimited cold store reachable by path. The tree-as-signpost trick means the agent can find a memory without paying tokens for its body. Git gives versioning, diffable memory edits, and cross-machine propagation for free.
patterns.build: Add hday_memory.py exposing a memory root (default .hermes-day/memory/, env override) with the layout system/{persona.md,human.md} + reference/*. Each file: YAML frontmatter (description) + body. pre_llm hook composes: (1) every file under system/ verbatim, (2) a deterministic tree listing (sorted, one line per path, no bodies) for everything else. Expose memory_read(path)/memory_write(path, body, frontmatter) tools that refuse paths outside the root. Persist via `git -C <root> commit -am <summary>` when git is present, else plain writes; never fail the turn on git errors. Emit a token count for the system/ section into the ledger so drift is visible.
patterns.test: tests/test_hday_memory.py::test_system_blocks_always_in_prompt_and_tree_is_paths_only — write system/persona.md + reference/deep.md, run a pre_llm pass, assert the prompt contains the persona body and the string 'reference/deep.md' but NOT its body; assert memory_read('../../etc/passwd') raises.

patterns.name: sleep-time-memory-consolidation
patterns.what: Two agents exist under the hood: a primary agent that CANNOT edit its own in-context memory, and a sleep-time agent that holds the memory-editing tools and can rewrite BOTH the primary's in-context memory and its own. Memory management therefore happens asynchronously, off the conversation's latency path. The sleep-time agent is typically configured with a stronger/slower model than the primary, and a frequency setting trades tokens for how often it revises learned context. Updates are 'anytime': the primary can read memory while the sleep-time agent is still reasoning. Motivation stated in the post: in MemGPT, memory management, conversation and other tasks are bundled in one agent, making it slower and less reliable, and incremental in-conversation memory formation becomes messy over time.
patterns.why: Removes memory-write latency and tool-choice ambiguity from the foreground agent, and lets a stronger model do the consolidation. 'Anytime' writes mean consolidation never blocks a read. The frequency knob turns consolidation into an explicit cost dial rather than an accident.
patterns.build: Split the memory tool surface: foreground sessions get memory_read + memory_append_note; only a consolidator lane gets memory_rewrite/merge/delete. Add a consolidator entry point (cron or post-turn, gated by a frequency budget in the ledger) that reads the session ledger + gotchas + notes and rewrites system/*.md. Never let the consolidator block a read: it writes to a temp file and atomically renames. Record each consolidation pass (model, tokens, files touched) in the decision ledger so 'stronger model for consolidation' is measurable.
patterns.test: tests/test_memory_consolidation.py::test_foreground_cannot_rewrite_blocks_and_consolidator_is_atomic — assert the foreground tool list excludes memory_rewrite; run a consolidator pass over a seeded ledger and assert system/*.md changed, the rename was atomic (no partial file observed), and a ledger row was appended.

patterns.name: subagent-frontmatter-memory-blocks
patterns.what: Subagents are Markdown files with YAML frontmatter in .letta/agents/ (project) or ~/.letta/agents/ (global): name, description, tools (allowlist, e.g. 'Glob, Grep, Read'), model, and memoryBlocks (which memory blocks the subagent may see, e.g. 'human, persona'). Built-ins are curated per-purpose: fork (inherits the parent conversation with full context and tools, model=inherit), general-purpose (read/write), recall (read-ONLY search of conversation history), reflection (background sleep-time consolidation), memory (reorganizes memory blocks into a cleaner hierarchy with less redundancy), init and history-analyzer. Each built-in has a recommended model tier (auto / auto-fast / inherit) and a read/write vs read-only access level.
patterns.why: Memory scope becomes a declarative property of the agent definition instead of an ambient global — a recall agent that cannot write is safe to run anywhere. Read-only-by-default for search agents plus an explicit reorg agent separates 'find it' from 'fix it'.
patterns.build: Define subagent specs as .hermes-day/agents/*.md with frontmatter {name, description, tools, model, memory_blocks, access: read|read-write}. A loader parses them into typed dicts validated at startup (unknown tool or block name = hard error). The router consults memory_blocks to decide which system/ blocks to inject into that subagent's context. Ship built-ins: recall (read-only, ledger+memory search), memory (reorg/dedupe blocks), reflection (background consolidation), fork (inherit parent trace). Mirror the frontmatter in the desktop cockpit so the agent roster is inspectable.
patterns.test: tests/test_agent_specs.py::test_recall_agent_is_read_only_and_unknown_block_fails_closed — load the shipped specs, assert the recall spec's access is read and its tool list contains no write tool; assert a spec naming memory_blocks: nonexistent raises at load time.

patterns.name: extraction-pipeline-with-dedup
patterns.what: add() runs a four-stage write pipeline: (1) context lookup — check related existing memories so the same fact is not stored twice; (2) fact extraction — an LLM extracts preferences, decisions, plans and reusable details; (3) deduplication and embedding — redundant facts are removed, each memory is embedded for semantic search; (4) entity extraction — pull the people/places/orgs/concepts each memory mentions, stored for entity matching at search time. Writes are ADDITIVE by default (new facts never silently rewrite old ones); infer=False stores raw content verbatim; corrections require explicit update/delete. Messages are the input, extracted facts are the storage unit, and scope is user_id / agent_id / run_id plus metadata filters.
patterns.why: Turns a chat transcript into clean, deduplicated, queryable facts — retrieval then works on facts rather than raw turns. Additivity is a correctness property: an inferred rewrite is an unreviewable mutation, so the safe default is append and let explicit ops correct.
patterns.build: Give the decision ledger a memory_add(messages, *, scope, infer=True, metadata) that runs: related-lookup (lexical + embedding over existing rows) -> extract (typed judgment returning a list of candidate facts) -> dedupe (drop near-duplicates by normalized-text hash then similarity) -> store with {scope, metadata, source_episode_id}. Keep infer=False as an escape hatch for verbatim capture. Never rewrite on add; expose memory_update/memory_delete as separate, ledger-logged ops. All writes go through the gate so an unmandated write is vetoed like any other side effect.
patterns.test: tests/test_memory_add.py::test_duplicate_facts_are_dropped_and_old_facts_survive — add the same preference twice and assert one row; add a contradicting preference and assert BOTH rows exist with distinct episode ids until an explicit update runs.

patterns.name: entity-graph-memory
patterns.what: Mem0 builds a graph where the entities mentioned across memories (people, places, organizations, concepts) become nodes and memories that share an entity become connected. No schema is defined by the developer and there is no external graph store to provision — it is built in and always on. The stated payoff is entity-centric questions ('what do we know about Alice?') answered from many separate conversations, and multi-hop recall linking a fact in one memory to a related fact in another. Entity extraction in the write pipeline is what feeds these nodes.
patterns.why: Pure vector retrieval cannot answer 'everything about X across all sessions' — that is a traversal, not a similarity. Deriving nodes from already-extracted entities means the graph costs one extra index rather than a second extraction pass.
patterns.build: Add an entities index alongside the memory store: {entity_key -> [memory_id]}, populated from the entity-extraction stage, with entity_key normalized (lowercased, trimmed, alias-merged). Add memory_recall_entity(entity, *, depth=1) that walks shared-entity edges and returns the connected memories with their episode ids. Depth is capped and every hop is recorded in the ledger. Start with an inverted index in SQLite; only reach for a real graph store if traversal depth > 2 is ever needed.
patterns.test: tests/test_memory_graph.py::test_entity_recall_links_across_sessions — seed two sessions that both mention the same project entity, assert memory_recall_entity returns both memories with distinct source episode ids, and assert depth=2 finds the transitive memory while depth=1 does not.

patterns.name: procedural-memory-type
patterns.what: memory_type on add() selects the kind of memory. Only procedural_memory is actually implemented: it stores step-by-step task knowledge (how an agent performs a workflow) rather than facts about a user, and requires an agent_id. The docs state plainly that semantic_memory and episodic_memory exist in the enum but are NOT wired into the extraction pipeline, are rejected by validation, and have no documented roadmap. Sync add() raises Mem0ValidationError; async raises ValueError.
patterns.why: A useful negative example: an enum that promises three memory types while one is real is worse than one type. It also shows the right home for 'how to do this task' knowledge — keyed to the AGENT, not the user, because a workflow belongs to the performer.
patterns.build: Add a procedures store keyed by agent/lane (not by user): a successful run's tool sequence, its preconditions and its outcome becomes a retrievable procedure. Wire it into hday_router.suggest so a repeated task shape recalls the procedure that worked, and expose the count of procedures in the cockpit. Reject unknown memory types at the API boundary with a typed error rather than silently accepting them — the documented failure mode here is exactly that class of bug.
patterns.test: tests/test_procedures.py::test_unknown_memory_type_is_rejected_and_procedure_recall_is_agent_scoped — assert an unknown memory_type raises a typed error naming the valid value; assert a procedure stored for lane A is not returned for lane B.

patterns.name: bitemporal-edge-validity
patterns.what: Edges carry a temporal validity window in BOTH event time and ingestion time: t_valid/t_invalid describe when the fact was true in the world, and t'_valid/t'_invalid describe when the system learned and superseded it. When a new edge contradicts an existing one, the existing edge is INVALIDATED — its t_invalid is set to the new edge's t_valid — rather than deleted or overwritten. The README frames the same model as a 'context graph': every fact has a validity window ('Kendra loves Adidas shoes (as of March 2026)'), entities evolve with updated summaries, and everything traces back to episodes. Retrieval filters expired edges; history is preserved for as-of queries.
patterns.why: Makes contradiction handling non-destructive: the system can answer both 'what is true now' and 'what did we believe last week', and an agent's stale belief is auditable rather than lost. It is the missing half of an append-only ledger — a ledger records what was written, a bitemporal graph records what stopped being true.
patterns.build: Extend ledger rows with four timestamps: valid_from/valid_to (when the decision was in force) and created_at/expired_at (when hermes-day recorded and superseded it). Add a supersede(old_id, new_id, reason) op that sets valid_to = new.valid_from and expired_at = now WITHOUT deleting the row. Default recall filters expired rows; add memory_as_of(ts) for point-in-time recall. Surface 'superseded' as a distinct cockpit badge so a stale belief is visible rather than silently absent.
patterns.test: tests/test_ledger_bitemporal.py::test_supersede_invalidates_without_deleting — write fact A, supersede it with B, assert A still exists with valid_to == B.valid_from, assert default recall returns only B, assert memory_as_of(before_B) returns only A.

patterns.name: episode-provenance
patterns.what: Every derived fact traces back to an EPISODE — the raw data as ingested, the ground-truth stream. The graph is built from episodes (text and structured JSON), and the ingestion pipeline is: initialize indices/constraints, add episodes, search edges with hybrid search, rerank by graph distance, search nodes with predefined search recipes. The paper's ingestion section adds that entity extraction processes the current message plus the last n messages (n=4 in the paper, i.e. two complete turns) for context, and that writes go through predefined Cypher queries rather than LLM-generated database queries, to keep schema formats consistent and reduce hallucination.
patterns.why: Provenance is what makes a memory layer auditable and re-derivable: if extraction improves, you can re-run it over the same episodes instead of losing the source. Predefined write queries over model-generated ones is the same lesson as hermes-day's own gate — deterministic surfaces over model discretion for anything that mutates state.
patterns.build: Give every memory row and every ledger row a source_episode_id pointing at an immutable episode record (session id, turn index, tool call id, or an explicit ingested artifact path). Episodes are append-only and never rewritten. Add memory_provenance(memory_id) -> episode chain for the cockpit, and a memory_rebuild(episode_id) that re-runs extraction for one episode. Keep the extraction write-path as fixed, typed operations (no model-authored SQL/JSON writes).
patterns.test: tests/test_provenance.py::test_every_memory_has_an_immutable_episode_and_rebuild_is_idempotent — assert no memory row can be created with a null source_episode_id; mutate the extractor prompt, re-run memory_rebuild for one episode and assert the episode record is byte-identical while derived rows changed.

patterns.name: hybrid-retrieval-plus-rerankers
patterns.what: Retrieval is search-then-rerank. Three search functions run: cosine semantic similarity, Okapi BM25 full-text (both via Neo4j's Lucene), and breadth-first search over the graph. The paper is explicit about why: full-text finds word similarity, cosine finds semantic similarity, and BFS finds CONTEXTUAL similarity (nodes/edges closer in the graph appeared in more similar conversational contexts); BFS is described as enhancing the initial search results. The rerank stage raises precision: RRF (reciprocal rank fusion) and MMR (maximal marginal relevance) are supported, plus a graph-based episode-mentions reranker that prioritizes results by how often an entity or fact is mentioned in episodes. Graphiti's README exposes the same shape as 'predefined search recipes' and 'rerank by graph distance'.
patterns.why: Different query shapes fail in different ways — an exact identifier needs BM25, a paraphrase needs cosine, a 'what is related to this' needs traversal. Reranking after a high-recall union is what makes the union safe. hermes-day's router already does lexical ranking; adding the other two channels plus a fusion step is the upgrade path.
patterns.build: Generalize hday_router.rank_wide into a recall pipeline: channel 1 = lexical_judge (exists), channel 2 = embedding cosine over memory + tool descriptions, channel 3 = BFS over the entity/decision graph (depth 1-2). Fuse with RRF (score = sum 1/(k + rank), k=60) then apply MMR to drop near-duplicates (lambda ~0.7 relevance vs diversity). Add an episode-mentions tiebreak using the provenance counts. Return the per-channel rank vector in Pick so the fusion is auditable, and keep a degraded path (lexical only) when no embedder is configured — mirroring hday_ctxscore's existing head/tail fallback.
patterns.test: tests/test_hybrid_recall.py::test_rrf_fuses_channels_and_mmr_drops_near_duplicates — stub three channels with disjoint rankings and assert the fused order matches a hand-computed RRF; feed two near-identical candidates and assert MMR keeps one; assert no-embedder config still returns lexical results.

patterns.name: community-summaries-label-propagation
patterns.what: Beyond entities and facts, the graph contains COMMUNITY nodes holding summaries derived through an iterative map-reduce-style summarization of member nodes. Communities are named with key terms and subjects from their summaries, and those names are embedded and stored so a query can reach a community. Updates are dynamic: when a new entity node is added, the system surveys the communities of neighbouring nodes, assigns the new node to the community held by the PLURALITY of its neighbours, then updates the community summary. The paper notes the tradeoff — dynamic updating is efficient but the resulting communities gradually drift, which is why the map-reduce rebuild exists alongside it.
patterns.why: Gives coarse, high-level retrieval for questions that no single fact answers ('what have we been working on this month'), and the plurality rule makes incremental assignment cheap and deterministic. Naming communities from their own summaries is what makes them findable without a separate classifier.
patterns.build: Add a periodic (cron) community pass over the decision ledger: cluster recent entries by shared entities/tags, summarize each cluster with the cheap model, store {community_id, name, summary, member_ids, embedding}. Incremental path: a new entry joins the community held by the plurality of its entity neighbours. Keep the derived-at timestamp and a drift counter so a full rebuild can be scheduled when the incremental assignments diverge. Expose communities as a retrieval channel for digest/cockpit 'what's been happening' views.
patterns.test: tests/test_communities.py::test_plurality_assignment_and_drift_flag — build three clusters, add a node adjacent to two of them, assert it joins the plurality community; force many incremental assignments and assert the drift counter trips the rebuild recommendation.

patterns.name: profiles-vs-collections
patterns.what: Semantic memory is stored in one of two shapes. A PROFILE is a single structured document holding current state (e.g. a user profile with preferences and other_preferences lists); it excels when you need quick access to current state, when you have data requirements about what may be stored, and it is easy to hand to a user for manual editing. A COLLECTION is many individual documents; it is right when you want to track knowledge across many interactions WITHOUT loss of information and when you want to recall information contextually rather than every time. The docs frame the choice as a decision, not a default.
patterns.why: The two shapes have opposite failure modes: a profile is always-loaded and therefore token-expensive and lossy (it summarizes), a collection is cheap and complete but only surfaces what you ask for. Making the choice explicit prevents the common drift into 'one giant memory blob'.
patterns.build: Implement both stores in hday_memory: a bounded profile document (system/profile.md, with a declared field schema and a hard token cap enforced at write time) and a collection table (many rows, retrieved on demand). Route writes by intent: corrections/preferences -> profile; observations/decisions/artifacts -> collection. Expose the profile in the cockpit as a human-editable pane, since that is its stated advantage.
patterns.test: tests/test_memory_shapes.py::test_profile_is_capped_and_collection_is_not — write past the profile's token cap and assert the write is rejected (or must evict a named field), while the collection accepts unbounded appends and only surfaces rows on query.

patterns.name: episodic-memory-schema
patterns.what: Episodic memory preserves successful interactions as learning examples. The documented schema is a typed Episode with four fields — observation ('the situation and relevant context'), thoughts ('key considerations and reasoning process'), action ('what was done in response'), result ('what happened and why it worked'). Extraction is configured by create_memory_manager(model, schemas=[Episode], instructions='Extract examples of successful interactions...', enable_inserts=True) and returns typed records (ExtractedMemory with an id and the Episode content). The docs stress the contrast with semantic memory: episodic captures the situation, the reasoning and WHY it worked, not just the fact.
patterns.why: A stored success without its reasoning cannot be reused — you get the what, not the when-to. The four-field schema forces the extractor to record the situation and the causal story, which is exactly what a later retrieval needs to judge applicability.
patterns.build: Add an episodic store whose rows are typed Episodes {observation, thoughts, action, result, outcome: success|failure, lane, tools_used, source_episode_id}. Populate it from finished turns (post_tool_call / turn-complete) only when the outcome is verified — tie it to the existing evidence verdict so unverified turns never become 'learning examples'. Recall episodes by situation similarity and inject at most 2 into pre_llm for a matching lane.
patterns.test: tests/test_episodic.py::test_only_verified_turns_become_episodes — feed one verified and one no-evidence turn, assert only the verified one yields an Episode row, and assert every Episode carries a non-empty result field.

patterns.name: procedural-prompt-optimizer
patterns.what: Procedural memory encodes how the agent should behave; it starts as the system prompt and then EVOLVES through feedback. create_prompt_optimizer(model, kind='metaprompt', config={'max_reflection_steps': 3}) takes trajectories paired with feedback (e.g. {"trajectories": [(trajectory, {"user_score": 0})], "prompt": prompt}) and returns a rewritten prompt. In the documented example the optimiser turns a bare 'You are a helpful assistant.' into a numbered behavioural rule list derived from the failure in the trajectory.
patterns.why: Turns prompt maintenance from an anecdote-driven edit into a repeatable, offline job driven by recorded outcomes. Heremes-day already records the outcomes (the ledger + evidence verdicts) — this is the missing consumer of that data.
patterns.build: Add an offline optimiser job that reads ledger rows for a lane, pairs each with a scalar outcome (verified=1, checks-failed=0, guard-veto=-1) plus the failure text, and rewrites that lane's instruction block via a metaprompt loop with max_reflection_steps capped (start at 3). Never auto-apply: write the candidate prompt + a diff to runs/prompt-candidates/<lane>-<ts>.md and require an explicit promote. Cap reflection steps and record token cost in the ledger.
patterns.test: tests/test_prompt_optimizer.py::test_optimizer_proposes_but_never_auto_applies — run the job over seeded ledger rows, assert a candidate file exists containing a diff against the live prompt, assert the live prompt file is byte-identical afterwards, and assert a promote step is required to change it.

patterns.name: typed-signature-contract
patterns.what: A Signature is the declarative contract between program and model: input fields, output fields, and instructions. Mechanically, every field is a pydantic FieldInfo and the base Signature extends pydantic.BaseModel, with DSPy metadata in json_schema_extra; any pydantic constraint (gt, lt, min_length) therefore works and gets stringified into json_schema_extra['constraints'] so the ADAPTER mentions it in the prompt. The class docstring becomes the instructions (cleandoc'd; if absent DSPy generates 'Given the fields X, produce the fields Y.'). Instructions live on the signature, not the module — the module (Predict/ChainOfThought/ReAct) supplies only the call-time strategy, so the same signature can be handed to any module. Field ORDER is meaningful: Signature.fields is what the adapter walks when rendering, so reordering changes the prompt.
patterns.why: One typed object that is simultaneously the schema, the prompt and the validation target — which is precisely the 'Jev-native' shape hermes-day wants for judgments. Because instructions are separable from the call strategy, you can swap a one-shot judgment for a chain-of-thought one without rewriting the task, and because constraints are pydantic, the validation is free.
patterns.build: Introduce hday_sig.py: a Signature base class (pydantic) with InputField/OutputField factories carrying desc and prefix, a docstring-derived instructions property, and deterministic field ordering (inputs then outputs). Rewrite the gate judge and router judgments to declare Signatures instead of free-form prompt strings. Render via an adapter so the SAME signature can be sent to different providers (see adapter-layer-coercion). Keep field names stable — see immutable-signature-optimizer-safety.
patterns.test: tests/test_hday_sig.py::test_signature_is_the_schema_and_the_prompt — declare a signature with a constrained field, assert the rendered prompt contains the docstring as instructions plus the constraint text, and assert a value violating the constraint fails pydantic validation rather than reaching the model.

patterns.name: immutable-signature-optimizer-safety
patterns.what: Every mutation method (with_instructions, with_updated_fields, prepend, append, insert, delete) deep-copies the field dict, applies the change and returns a NEW Signature class — the original is untouched. The stated reason: optimizers run many candidate variants of the same program, and in-place mutation would let candidates clobber each other through shared state. Two more rules matter: field names and desc/prefix are INERT to instruction optimizers (GEPA rewrites only the docstring, because field names are the program's public interface — caller code reads result.haiku), and equality for comparing variants is Signature.equals(other), not ==, which compares class identity. Persistence round-trips only the mutable parts: dump_state()/load_state() save instructions plus each field's annotation, prefix, desc and field-type tag.
patterns.why: This is the safety model for self-modifying prompts: candidates must be values, not mutations, or a bad optimisation silently corrupts the live program. The 'field names are inert' rule is the boundary that keeps an optimizer from breaking callers — a boundary hermes-day needs before it lets anything rewrite its own instructions.
patterns.build: Make hermes-day's instruction blocks immutable values: with_instructions(block, text) returns a new block object; a candidate is a (base_hash, diff) pair. Never let an optimiser touch tool names, lane names or field names — only the instruction text, with the same explicit rationale documented in the module. Persist candidates as dump_state()-style dicts (instructions + field metadata) so a promoted prompt can be loaded without re-declaring code.
patterns.test: tests/test_prompt_immutability.py::test_candidate_mutation_cannot_touch_the_live_prompt_or_field_names — apply a candidate that tries to rename a field and assert the rename is rejected; assert the live prompt object's hash is unchanged after evaluating 3 candidates.

patterns.name: gepa-reflective-pareto
patterns.what: GEPA (Genetic-Pareto, arxiv 2507.19457) evolves textual components using REFLECTION rather than reinforcement. Documented mechanics: it captures full traces of the module's execution, identifies the trace parts corresponding to a specific predictor, and reflects on that predictor's behaviour to propose a new instruction for it. Users supply rich TEXTUAL feedback in addition to scalar metric scores, at the granularity of individual predictors or the whole system. Candidate selection is Pareto-based over per-instance scores (candidate_selection_strategy: 'pareto' | 'current_best'), with reflection_minibatch_size (default 3), auto budgets ('light'|'medium'|'heavy'), max_metric_calls/max_full_evals, skip_perfect_score=True, add_format_failure_as_feedback, and pluggable instruction_proposer/code_proposer. It can also be used as inference-time search (valset=trainset, track_stats=True) returning the Pareto frontier via detailed_results.
patterns.why: Scalar-only optimisation cannot tell the optimiser WHY a case failed, so it converges slowly and overfits the aggregate; textual feedback carries the diagnosis. Pareto selection keeps variants that are best on DIFFERENT slices instead of collapsing to one average-best, which is what a gate with several distinct failure modes (over-blocking, under-blocking, false honesty flags) actually needs.
patterns.build: Build a GEPA-shaped optimiser for the gate's judge instructions: metric returns (score, feedback_text) where feedback quotes the vetoed command and the human-readable reason; the Pareto frontier is tracked per failure family (over-block / under-block / wrong-mandate / honesty-guard). Minibatch = 3 real ledger cases, budget capped by max_metric_calls, skip_perfect_score on. Log the frontier to the ledger; promotion stays manual. Keep the existing deterministic regex honesty guard untouched — optimise only the JUDGE prompt.
patterns.test: tests/test_gepa_frontier.py::test_pareto_keeps_slice_best_candidates_and_budget_is_enforced — with two candidate prompts each best on a different failure family, assert both survive the frontier; assert the run stops at max_metric_calls and that no candidate run mutates the live judge prompt.

patterns.name: adapter-layer-coercion
patterns.what: A signature only DECLARES types; coercion happens in the adapter layer. dspy/adapters/utils.py::parse_value tries json_repair first, falls back to ast.literal_eval, then validates against TypeAdapter(annotation); for custom dspy.Type subclasses it retries with the raw string when pydantic validation fails so the type's own parser can take over. The stated reason for the split: multiple adapters (Chat, JSON, XML, TwoStep) must coerce the same Signature differently — a JSON adapter leans on the model's JSON mode, an XML adapter parses from tags — so keeping coercion in the adapter keeps signatures lean and avoids duplicated parser logic. Field values arrive as strings and are cast at the edge.
patterns.why: This is the concrete answer to 'provider-agnostic structured output': the contract is declared once and each provider gets the rendering and parsing strategy it is actually good at, with a documented fallback chain for malformed output instead of a single brittle json.loads.
patterns.build: Add hday_adapters.py with a 3-rung parse chain (json_repair -> ast.literal_eval -> TypeAdapter) plus per-provider adapters: JSON-mode for providers that support it, a tag-based adapter for providers that do not, and a prompted-schema adapter as the last resort. Record which rung succeeded in the ledger — a rising share of json_repair hits is an early warning that a provider's structured output is degrading.
patterns.test: tests/test_adapters.py::test_parse_chain_recovers_malformed_json_and_records_the_rung — feed trailing-comma and single-quoted payloads and assert both coerce; assert the ledger row records the rung; assert a value that no rung can repair raises rather than silently returning None.

patterns.name: typed-deps-runcontext
patterns.what: The Agent takes deps_type=<a type> (the TYPE, not an instance — it is not used at runtime, it exists for full type checking), and each run passes the matching instance as deps=. Dependencies are accessed through RunContext[Deps], which must be the first parameter of system-prompt functions, tools and output validators; accessing them is ctx.deps.<field>. RunContext is parameterised with the deps type so a mismatch is a static type error, and it also exposes .agent (name, output_type) and realtime properties. Synchronous dependency functions are run via run_in_executor in a thread pool; deps fields can be referenced in instructions via template strings (TemplateStr('Hello {{name}}')). Dependencies can be overridden, which is what makes the agent testable.
patterns.why: Explicit, typed injection replaces ambient globals — a tool declares exactly what it needs, tests pass fakes, and a typo is caught by the type checker instead of at 3am. It is also the mechanism that keeps a tool's contract honest, since the deps are the tool's entire outside world.
patterns.build: Introduce a DayDeps dataclass {repo_root, ledger, config, clock, embedder} and make every hermes-day tool/hook take ctx: RunContext[DayDeps] as its first argument instead of reading module globals or env. Declare deps_type once at registration so a mismatch fails type-check. Use override to inject a frozen clock and an in-memory ledger in tests — this removes the monkeypatch-heavy setup visible in the current test suite.
patterns.test: tests/test_day_deps.py::test_tools_take_typed_deps_and_override_replaces_them — assert a tool invoked without ctx raises; run a lane with overridden deps (frozen clock, in-memory ledger) and assert no real filesystem or clock access occurred.

patterns.name: output-retry-budgets-retrypromptpart
patterns.what: Retries are budgeted separately for tools and output: Agent(retries=3) sets both, Agent(retries={'tools': 5, 'output': 1}) sets them individually, and a bare int sets both; unspecified keys keep a default of 1. A retry is a MODEL REQUEST carrying a RetryPromptPart that holds the failure as a string (from ModelRetry) or a list of pydantic error details (from ValidationError) and renders with 'Fix the errors and try again.' appended; its tool_name is set for a tool-call retry and None for an output retry. Tool retries are triggered by a ValidationError on the arguments, by the tool/args_validator/hook raising ModelRetry, by a tool timeout, or by the model calling a tool that does not exist. Counter semantics are precise: the counter is keyed by tool name and RESETS ON SUCCESS (so a tool alternating fail/success never exhausts a budget of 1), max_retries=N means N retries / N+1 attempts, and a hallucinated tool name gets its own budget under the invented name, bounded by the agent-wide tools budget. Budget exhaustion raises UnexpectedModelBehavior. ToolFailed is the deliberate opposite of a retry: it records a ToolReturnPart with outcome='failed' and does NOT consume the budget, so repeated failures are bounded by UsageLimits instead. Retry prompts stay in the history, so reusing that history replays earlier failures to the model (filter them with a ProcessHistory capability if unwanted).
patterns.why: Gives an exact, testable retry contract instead of an ad-hoc loop: separate budgets for 'the model wrote bad JSON' and 'the model chose a bad action', counters that cannot be silently exhausted by a flaky tool, and a first-class way to report a failure that is NOT a retry. The reset-on-success rule is the subtle one — it prevents a retry storm being masked by interleaved successes.
patterns.build: Give hermes-day's typed judgments a retry budget object {tools: N, output: M} with the same counter keying (per tool name, reset on success) and the same two failure channels: a repair prompt that replays the pydantic error list, and an explicit 'failed, do not retry' result that bypasses the budget. On budget exhaustion raise a typed error naming the tool/budget. Store the retry prompt in the transcript so a resumed session sees its earlier mistakes, and expose the per-tool retry counts in the ledger.
patterns.test: tests/test_retry_budgets.py::test_counters_reset_on_success_and_exhaustion_raises — drive a tool fail/succeed/fail/succeed with budget 1 and assert no exhaustion; drive fail/fail with budget 1 and assert a typed budget error; assert the 'failed' channel never increments the counter.

patterns.name: retry-budget-multiplication
patterns.what: The docs decompose worst-case request volume into three independent multipliers: N = model requests per logical call (initial attempt, one follow-up per tool call — even a successful tool call queues another request — plus retry prompts); M = attempts per model request inside the provider SDK client (e.g. an OpenAI client with max_retries=2 allows 3); K = attempts per request on the wire (transport stop strategy, e.g. stop_after_attempt(2) means 2 total). The worked example: retries={'output': 2} x SDK max_retries=2 x stop_after_attempt(2) puts 3 x 3 x 2 = 18 requests on the network, each carrying its own timeout, i.e. 180 seconds of request time worst case before backoff. The docs also warn that UsageLimits.request_limit (default 50) bounds only N and never sees the wire requests added beneath it.
patterns.why: A budget that multiplies to 18x is a budget you cannot reason about — and this is exactly the class of bug that makes an agent look 'hung' or mysteriously expensive. Making the multiplication explicit turns a hidden cost into a computed, assertable number.
patterns.build: Add a worst-case request estimator to the cost guard: given (turns, tools per turn, output_retries, sdk_max_retries, transport_attempts, timeout) compute N*M*K and the worst-case wall time, and refuse configurations above a declared ceiling before the run starts. Surface the estimate on the cockpit card for long-running lanes. This is a pure function and needs no network to test.
patterns.test: tests/test_retry_math.py::test_worst_case_request_count_and_refusal — assert (3,3,2) computes 18 and the derived wall time; assert a configuration above the ceiling is refused before any request is issued.

patterns.name: reask-validation-loop
patterns.what: Frames self-critique as ordinary validation: 'Instead of framing self-critique or self-reflection in AI as new concepts, we can view them as validation errors with clear error messages that the system can use to self-correct.' Validators are pydantic validators (field_validator / AfterValidator / BeforeValidator) that raise ValueError; the failure is caught and the model is re-asked. The documented mechanics behind the scenes: the client appends the assistant message, then appends a user message reading 'Please correct the function call; errors encountered:\n{e}' — i.e. the raw pydantic error text is the repair prompt — and loops up to max_retries (example sets 2). The docs describe this as a defence against two failure forms: pydantic validation errors (code- or LLM-based) and JSON decoding errors.
patterns.why: Reuses an existing, well-tested validation framework instead of inventing a reflection loop, and makes the repair signal the actual error text rather than a vague 'try again'. It is also the cheapest possible structured-output retry: no new prompt template per task.
patterns.build: Implement hermes-day judgments as pydantic models with real validators (e.g. a risk score bounded 0..1, a lane name that must exist in the registry, a verdict that must cite at least one evidence id) and a reask loop that replays the pydantic error text verbatim, capped by the retry budget above. Log every reask with the validator that fired, so 'which rule does the model keep violating' becomes a queryable fact rather than a hunch.
patterns.test: tests/test_reask.py::test_invalid_judgment_is_reasked_with_the_pydantic_error_text — return an out-of-range risk score, assert the follow-up request contains the validator's message, assert the loop stops at the budget and raises, and assert the ledger records the fired validator.

patterns.name: llm-validator-with-context
patterns.what: Two mechanisms combine. (1) llm_validator(rule, client=...) plugs a model-based check into the same pydantic pipeline via BeforeValidator, so a semantic rule ('don't say objectionable things') raises a ValidationError like any other validator — and the docs note the resulting error message is generated by the LLM, not the code, 'so it'll be helpful for re-asking the model'. (2) The context parameter passes runtime data to validators, read via ValidationInfo (info.context): the worked example validates that a supporting_quote actually appears in a supplied source_text, after whitespace normalization — a deterministic, non-LLM check against ground truth.
patterns.why: Two different jobs, correctly separated: model-based checks for judgment-style rules that cannot be coded, and deterministic checks against runtime ground truth for anything checkable. The context channel is what makes the deterministic half possible, and it is the anti-hallucination mechanism hermes-day needs for citation-style claims.
patterns.build: Wire the ledger's evidence into validation context: any judgment that cites a file, a test name or an evidence id is validated against the real artifact (path exists, test name appears in the run output) via ValidationInfo-style context, deterministically. Reserve llm_validator-style checks for genuinely subjective rules and mark them as such in the ledger so a model-judged failure is never confused with a code-judged one.
patterns.test: tests/test_grounded_validation.py::test_citation_validators_check_real_artifacts_and_are_marked — assert a cited file that does not exist fails validation with a code-generated message; assert the ledger distinguishes code-judged from llm-judged failures.

patterns.name: constrained-decoding-fsm
patterns.what: Outlines accepts an output TYPE alongside the prompt and guarantees the generated text conforms to it. Supported types span the Python ecosystem: native types (int, str, float, bool), typing constructs (Literal, List, Dict, Enum, Union, Optional, Tuple, nested collections), and third-party types such as pydantic models; plus three library-specific ones — Choice(list) for DYNAMIC multiple choice, JsonSchema, Regex, and CFG (context-free grammars). Classification is done with Literal or Enum. Important contract detail: an Outlines generator ALWAYS returns a string — you cast it yourself (e.g. Character.model_validate_json(result)). The docs frame it as 'provide as an output type what you would give as the type hint of the return type of a function'.
patterns.why: Structural validity is enforced during generation rather than repaired after it, which removes the entire malformed-JSON failure class for local models. Choice() built from a runtime list is the piece hermes-day needs, because its lane/tool registry is not known at authoring time.
patterns.build: For the self-hosted/local-model path, render each judgment's output type as a grammar: a Choice built at runtime from the live lane registry for lane selection, a bounded int/float for scores, and a pydantic JSON schema for structured verdicts. Keep the adapter parse chain as a second line of defence for providers without grammar support, and assert in the ledger which enforcement path was used per call.
patterns.test: tests/test_constrained_output.py::test_runtime_choice_grammar_rejects_unknown_lane — build the Choice from a 3-lane registry, assert the generated lane is always one of the three and that a removed lane is no longer generatable; assert the returned value is a string that must be cast.

patterns.name: code-as-action
patterns.what: In a CodeAgent the model writes its action as executable code rather than a JSON blob of tool names and arguments; ToolCallingAgent (JSON/text actions) is still supported alongside it. The blog's stated advantages of code actions: composability (you can nest and reuse actions the way you define and call a Python function, which JSON cannot express), object management (storing an action's output such as a generated image), generality (code expresses anything a computer can do), and representation in LLM training data (plenty of quality code is already in the training set, so models are already fluent in it). It cites multiple papers on tool calling in code and points at Executable Code Actions Elicit Better LLM Agents.
patterns.why: One action can do what a dozen JSON tool calls do, because loops, conditionals and intermediate variables live in the action instead of the transcript. That is a direct context-length win for hermes-day, where multi-step triage currently costs a tool call per step.
patterns.build: Add a code-action lane for multi-step read-only work (triage a batch of findings, aggregate a ledger slice): the model emits one Python snippet against a small, documented API surface, hermes-day executes it in the interpreter below, and only the result enters the transcript. Gate it read-only by default and require the same mandate check as any write.
patterns.test: tests/test_code_actions.py::test_one_code_action_replaces_n_calls_and_is_read_only — assert a batch aggregation completes in a single action with one transcript entry, and that a write attempt inside a code action is vetoed by the gate.

patterns.name: ast-walking-interpreter
patterns.what: Code execution is not delegated to the vanilla Python interpreter; smolagents ships a LocalPythonExecutor that loads the Abstract Syntax Tree from the code and executes it operation by operation under explicit rules. Documented rules: imports are DISALLOWED unless explicitly added to an authorization list; access to submodules is disabled by default and each must be authorized individually (or a wildcard like 'numpy.*' to allow numpy and all subpackages) — with the noted trap that seemingly innocuous packages like random can expose harmful submodules (random._os); and the total count of elementary operations is capped to prevent infinite loops and resource bloating. The docs enumerate the threat model explicitly: plain LLM error, supply-chain compromise, prompt injection from a browsed page, and exploitation of publicly accessible agents.
patterns.why: An AST-walking executor gives a real allowlist boundary (what may be imported) plus a resource boundary (how much may run), and both are checkable without containers. The submodule trap is worth stealing verbatim: allowing a package is not the same as allowing its reachable modules.
patterns.build: Implement the code-action executor as an AST walker: no import unless on the allowlist, submodule access denied unless explicitly granted, an operation-count ceiling per action, and no attribute access to dunder names. Record every denied node in the ledger as a guard event so injection attempts are visible rather than silent. Keep the E2B-style remote sandbox as an optional escalation for anything that genuinely needs network or a full filesystem.
patterns.test: tests/test_code_executor.py::test_imports_and_submodules_are_denied_by_default_and_op_count_is_capped — assert 'import os' is denied, assert an authorized 'numpy' does not grant 'numpy.random' without the wildcard, assert an infinite loop trips the operation cap, and assert each denial appends a ledger guard event.

patterns.name: typed-step-memory-and-planning-step
patterns.what: Every agent in smolagents derives from a single MultiStepAgent class implementing the ReAct cycle (Yao et al., 2022). The loop is precisely specified: initialization stores the system prompt in a SystemPromptStep and the user query in a TaskStep; then, while the task is unsolved, the agent (a) calls agent.write_memory_to_messages() to serialize the agent logs into LLM-readable chat messages, (b) sends them to a Model and parses the completion into an action (a JSON blob for ToolCallingAgent, a code snippet for CodeAgent), (c) executes the action and logs the result as an ActionStep, and (d) runs every callback in agent.step_callbacks. When planning is activated the plan is PERIODICALLY REVISED and stored in a PlanningStep, which also feeds facts about the task into memory. Memory is therefore a typed, ordered log of step records rather than a message list, and serialization is an explicit, replaceable method. The docs also note the two variants fit different work: CodeAgent for code actions, ToolCallingAgent (JSON) when the work needs waiting between actions, e.g. web browsing with page-interaction latency.
patterns.why: A typed step log makes the transcript inspectable and compactable by step KIND rather than by message role — you can drop Observation payloads while keeping PlanningSteps and failed ActionSteps, which is exactly the policy the context-engineering patterns want. write_memory_to_messages as a single serialization seam is what makes 'render the same memory differently per provider' possible, and step_callbacks is a first-class hook point that hermes-day's post_tool_call currently approximates.
patterns.build: Replace the ad-hoc message list in a session with typed step records: SystemPromptStep, TaskStep, ActionStep {thought, action, observation, outcome}, PlanningStep {plan, facts}. Persist them in the ledger and render through one write_memory_to_messages() function that hday_adapters can vary per provider. Expose step_callbacks as the single hook surface (folding in post_tool_call), and emit a PlanningStep on a cadence (or when the plan drifts) that re-states the plan and the facts — the same recitation mechanism as 9.1, but recorded as a typed step so it is auditable.
patterns.test: tests/test_step_memory.py::test_steps_are_typed_ordered_and_planning_recites — run a 3-step task and assert the log order is [SystemPrompt, Task, Action, Action, Planning, Action]; assert dropping ActionStep observations leaves PlanningStep and failed ActionSteps intact; assert every step round-trips through write_memory_to_messages.

patterns.name: compaction-with-preserve-list-and-recitation
patterns.what: Compaction takes a conversation nearing the context limit, summarizes it, and reinitiates a new context window with the summary. In Claude Code the message history is passed to the model to summarize and compress the most critical details: the summary PRESERVES architectural decisions, unresolved bugs and implementation details while DISCARDING redundant tool outputs and messages, and the agent then continues with that summary plus the five most recently accessed files. Tuning advice: start by maximizing recall so the compaction prompt captures every relevant piece, then iterate to improve precision — over-aggressive compaction loses subtle context whose importance only appears later. The companion technique is structured note-taking (agentic memory): the agent writes notes persisted OUTSIDE the context window and pulls them back later, which is what lets an agent read its own notes and continue multi-hour work after a context reset.
patterns.why: The preserve list is the whole mechanism — an unguided 'summarize this' loses exactly the decisions that matter. Notes-outside-the-window make continuity survive the compaction boundary, so the summary does not have to carry everything.
patterns.build: Replace hday_ctxscore's generic vacuum with a compaction pass that takes an explicit preserve list (open decisions, vetoed commands and their reasons, unresolved failures, file paths touched, the current mandate) and discards raw tool payloads. Always re-inject the live plan/notes file AFTER the summary so it lands in the recent attention span (this is Manus's recitation trick: rewriting the todo list at the end of context pushes the global plan into the recent attention window and mitigates lost-in-the-middle). Add a compaction recall probe: a small set of questions whose answers must survive the summary, run in tests.
patterns.test: tests/test_compaction_recall.py::test_preserve_list_survives_and_plan_is_recited_last — compact a synthetic long trace and assert the open decision, the veto reason and the touched paths are present; assert the plan block is the LAST block in the rebuilt context; assert the recall probe passes.

patterns.name: tool-result-clearing
patterns.what: The cookbook's three context levers are compaction, tool-result clearing and memory. Tool clearing caps in-session token growth when the context is dominated by large, re-fetchable tool results (file reads, API responses). The API table gives the concrete knobs: clear_tool_uses_20250919, triggered by a server-side token threshold, with trigger (default 100K tokens), keep (default 3 tool uses), clear_at_least, exclude_tools and clear_tool_inputs. Compaction (compact_20260112) is separately triggered (default 150K, server-side minimum 50K) and exposes trigger, instructions and pause_after_compaction. The memory tool (memory_20250818) is different again: it is driven by the MODEL as a tool call, and the client implements the operations view, create, str_replace, insert, delete, rename against a /memories path. The cookbook's framing is that these are distinct primitives for distinct problems — bulky re-fetchable reads (clearing), long analytical conversations (compaction), knowledge that must survive between sessions (memory) — and it recommends replacing the default compaction prompt to preserve what your agent needs.
patterns.why: Tool results are usually the bulk of a long transcript and are the safest thing to drop because they are re-fetchable by construction. Clearing before compacting is the cheap win: no summarization call, no loss of the decision trail.
patterns.build: Extend hday_ctxscore's vacuum with a clearing stage that runs BEFORE any summarization: when the transcript crosses a token trigger, drop tool results older than the last N (start with 3), never touching assistant text, decisions or gate events; support an exclude list for tools whose results are not re-fetchable (e.g. one-shot probes) and a clear_at_least floor so clearing actually fires rather than no-oping. Keep the cleared payloads in the existing archive (hday_ctxscore already preserves hidden chunks) and leave a one-line pointer with the tool name + arguments so the agent can re-fetch.
patterns.test: tests/test_tool_clearing.py::test_old_tool_results_are_cleared_but_decisions_and_excluded_tools_survive — build a transcript with 6 tool results, assert the oldest 3 are replaced by pointers, assert assistant decisions and an excluded tool's result are intact, and assert the cleared payloads are still readable from the archive.

patterns.name: subagent-context-isolation-and-shared-traces
patterns.what: Anthropic: specialized sub-agents handle focused tasks with clean context windows while the main agent coordinates with a high-level plan; a subagent may explore with tens of thousands of tokens but returns only a condensed, distilled summary (often 1,000-2,000 tokens), so the detailed search context stays isolated and the lead agent synthesizes. Cognition argues the complementary constraint: PRINCIPLE 1 — share context, and share full agent traces, not just individual messages; PRINCIPLE 2 — actions carry implicit decisions, and conflicting decisions carry bad results. Their worked failure: two parallel subagents given the same task produce a Super-Mario background and a non-Flappy-Bird bird, because each acted on assumptions the other could not see. Their default is a single-threaded linear agent; their scaling answer is a dedicated model that compresses a history of actions and conversation into key details, events and decisions — 'hard to get right', and something they have fine-tuned a smaller model for. They also observe that Claude Code's subagents never run in parallel with the parent and are usually only asked to answer a question, not write code.
patterns.why: The two sources together define the contract: isolation is safe for INVESTIGATION and unsafe for WORK that must agree with other work. Heremes-day already spawns parallel lanes, so this is the rule that decides which of them may act. And the compressed-summary interface is the same object as the compaction preserve list.
patterns.build: Codify two subagent classes in hermes-day: (a) read-only investigators (recall/history/artifact search) that may run in parallel and MUST return a bounded summary (cap it — start at ~1.5K tokens) plus cited evidence ids; (b) writers that run single-threaded against the shared trace and are never parallel with a peer that touches the same artifact. Dispatch for a writer carries the full parent trace (not a paraphrase). Add a summary-size assertion so an investigator that returns a transcript is rejected. Surface the class (investigator vs writer) on the cockpit card.
patterns.test: tests/test_subagent_contract.py::test_investigators_are_bounded_and_writers_serialize — assert an investigator returning an over-cap summary is rejected; assert two writers touching the same artifact cannot be scheduled concurrently; assert a writer's dispatch payload contains the parent trace, not a summary.

patterns.name: kv-cache-stable-prefix-and-mask-dont-remove
patterns.what: Two rules from the Manus post. (1) Design around the KV-cache: the cache hit rate is called the single most important metric for a production agent, and cached input tokens can cost ~10x less than uncached. Practices: keep the prompt PREFIX stable (a common mistake is a second-precision timestamp at the top of the system prompt, which kills the cache from that token on), make the context APPEND-ONLY (avoid modifying previous actions/observations; ensure deterministic serialization, since many JSON serializers do not guarantee stable key ordering), and mark cache breakpoints explicitly when the provider needs them, at minimum covering the end of the system prompt. Agent workloads are prefill-dominated (they cite a ~100:1 input-to-output token ratio). (2) Mask, don't remove: avoid dynamically adding or removing tools mid-iteration, because tool definitions live near the front of the context so any change invalidates the cache for everything after it, and because previous actions referring to now-undefined tools confuse the model into schema violations or hallucinated actions. Instead mask token logits during decoding, or use response prefill — auto (prefill the assistant prefix), required (prefill to the tool-call token), specified (prefill into the function name). They also keep consistent action-name prefixes (browser_, shell_) so a whole group can be enforced without stateful logits processors.
patterns.why: Two cheap, high-leverage rules hermes-day currently violates: any per-turn timestamp or reordered block at the top of the prompt silently destroys caching, and a router that mutates the tool list per turn destroys it again AND confuses the model about its own history. Masking gets the same steering with neither cost.
patterns.build: In the prompt assembler: freeze the prefix (system + tool definitions) across turns, move anything volatile (clock, counters, current file) BELOW the stable block, and assert deterministic serialization (sorted keys) in a test. Add a cache-bust detector that hashes the prefix each turn and logs a warning to the ledger when it changes without a declared reason — the same shape as the existing 'warn on cache busts' idea. For routing, keep the full tool list in the prefix permanently and let hday_router express availability as a mask/allowlist applied at selection time rather than by rewriting the tool block; enforce group-level availability through consistent name prefixes.
patterns.test: tests/test_prefix_stability.py::test_prefix_hash_is_stable_across_turns_and_mask_does_not_rewrite_tools — run three turns with a changing clock and assert the prefix hash is identical; assert the rendered tool block is byte-identical while the router's allowed set changes; assert a deliberate prefix change logs a cache-bust event.

patterns.name: externalize-dont-delete
patterns.what: Manus treats the file system as the ultimate context: unlimited, persistent, directly operable by the agent, and used not just as storage but as structured externalized memory. Their compression strategies are always designed to be RESTORABLE — a web page's content can be dropped from context as long as the URL is preserved, and a document's contents can be omitted if its path remains available in the sandbox — so context shrinks without permanently losing information. They explicitly reject irreversible compression: an agent must predict its next action from all prior state, and you cannot reliably predict which observation becomes critical ten steps later. The companion rule is 'keep the wrong stuff in': leave failed actions and the resulting stack traces in the context, because erasing failure removes the evidence and the model then cannot update its beliefs away from the bad action; they call error recovery one of the clearest indicators of true agentic behaviour. Anthropic's framing matches from the other side: prefer just-in-time retrieval over pre-loading, keep lightweight identifiers (file paths, queries, links) and load data at runtime, with the file tree itself acting as a signpost system.
patterns.why: Both rules replace deletion with a pointer, which is what makes aggressive context reduction safe. Heremes-day's honesty guard already depends on failures being visible — if the transcript cleaned up vetoes and failed checks, the guard's whole signal would disappear.
patterns.build: Make every compression in hday_ctxscore restorable by construction: replace payloads with typed pointers {kind: file|url|tool_result|episode, ref, sha, bytes} and never drop the pointer. Add a hard rule (enforced in code, not convention) that gate vetoes, failed checks and error traces are never eligible for clearing or summarization — they are pinned like decisions. Add a rehydrate(pointer) tool so any cleared payload can be pulled back on demand, and count rehydrations in the ledger: a high rehydration rate on a specific pointer kind is evidence the compressor is dropping something it should have kept.
patterns.test: tests/test_restorable_compression.py::test_every_cleared_payload_keeps_a_working_pointer_and_failures_are_pinned — clear a long transcript and assert every dropped payload has a pointer that rehydrates byte-identically; assert gate vetoes and failed checks are still verbatim in context; assert rehydration counts land in the ledger.
